articles.title: US could play role in united Ireland push after Trump's backing, Irish PM says
articles.summary: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially help in a future push for a united Ireland after Trump backed it.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Nearly three decades after the Good Friday Agreement transformed Northern Ireland, Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially play a role in a future push for a united Ireland following President Donald Trump's backing for reunification. Martin, whose Fianna Fáil party supports Irish unity, said the landmark 1998 agreement – which largely ended 30 years of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as "the Troubles" – created a peaceful mechanism for deciding Northern Ireland's constitutional future, but cautioned that the deep divide between Northern Ireland's nationalist and unionist communities must first be bridged. "I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland." "The U.S. were critical to the success of peace and conflict resolution in Ireland," Martin added. IRISH PM REJECTS ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS IN IRELAND AMID DRAMATIC VOTE OVER BOYCOTTING ISRAEL GAME Martin spoke to Fox News Digital during the U.N. General Assembly in New York at what he described as a global "crossroad," with war raging in Ukraine, conflict across the Middle East and negotiations underway over Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Throughout the interview, he repeatedly returned to Ireland's own experience of conflict and peace as a guide to how the country approaches crises abroad, while defending the country's longstanding policy of military neutrality despite its growing support for Ukraine. The constitutional question of Irish unity gained renewed attention during Trump's recent visit to Ireland last month, when the president said he would "love" to see Ireland unified and predicted it would eventually happen. Asked during the Fox News Digital whether Washington could play a role again if Ireland eventually moves toward reunification, Martin replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah." Martin spoke before the latest confrontation over Garvaghy Road erupted in Portadown, Northern Ireland, reviving one of Northern Ireland's most bitter marching disputes and underscoring how potent nationalist-unionist divisions remain. The Parades Commission last month approved a limited Orange Order march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road for the first time in 28 years. Residents and supporters blocked the route, while police declined to force the parade through amid fears of serious disorder. The Orange Order is a Protestant organization whose members generally support Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, while many residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road community, who are predominantly Catholic, favor a united Ireland. The standoff has since spilled into the courts and Stormont, where parliament meets, as efforts to broker a compromise continue. Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum can be called if it appears a majority in Northern Ireland would support reunification. But Martin said more work is needed to define what a united Ireland would look like and deepen engagement on both sides of the border. IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND ‘NOT OVERRUN’ BY IMMIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS UKRAINE AND THE SEARCH FOR PEACE For Martin, however, the lessons of Northern Ireland's peace process extend far beyond the island. "Because of our conflict in Northern Ireland, we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway," Martin said. He said Ireland's experience ending decades of violence now shapes how it approaches Russia's war in Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East and Europe's increasingly uncertain security environment. "We don't get a sense that Russia is really interested at this particular stage," Martin said of efforts to end the war in Ukraine. Martin, who had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the previous evening, nevertheless argued that continued channels between Washington and Moscow were important. Asked whether a realistic peace settlement would ultimately require Ukraine to surrender territory to Russia, Martin rejected the premise. "Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. But he said a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations. "If we even could get a ceasefire on existing lines, and then negotiations to start," Martin said, adding that Kyiv would need protections against renewed Russian aggression. "Ukraine needs security guarantees." Martin also pointed to Ukraine's path toward European Union membership as potentially providing an additional layer of security and said the broader security architecture between Europe and Russia would ultimately have to be addressed in negotiations. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory," Martin said. HOW NEUTRAL IS IRELAND? Ireland's extensive support for Kyiv, however, raises a more contentious question at home: how far can a militarily neutral country support one side in a war while maintaining that neutrality? Ireland has committed more than $754 million in humanitarian assistance, military training and other non-lethal support to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 while stopping short of providing lethal weapons. Fox News Digital asked Martin whether that level of support undermined Ireland's neutrality. "No, because we don't give lethal aid, we haven't given military weaponry, but we have given non-lethal assistance in terms of training and so on like that, and also humanitarian aid to Ukraine," Martin said. Ireland has also taken in large numbers of Ukrainians fleeing the war. Martin said more than 120,000 had arrived at one point, with roughly 80,000 remaining in the country at the time of the interview. "That's not taking sides, that's taking humanitarian response to a war," Martin said. "And many are contributing, many are working in the economy." Ireland's neutrality has also faced scrutiny over the long-standing use of Shannon Airport by the U.S. military. NATO's top military commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, described Shannon in August as a "very important logistics hub" for the United States and said withdrawing American military access would probably damage U.S.-Irish relations. The airport's role has long drawn protests from Irish neutrality campaigners, who argue that allowing U.S. military personnel and aircraft to transit through a civilian airport undermines the country's neutral status. Despite differing approaches to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, Martin described the U.S.-Ireland relationship in almost familial terms. "There's a very strong bond between Ireland and the United States," Martin said. He pointed to the long-standing tradition of Irish leaders visiting the White House on St. Patrick's Day and the enormous Irish-American diaspora, which he estimated at roughly 30 million people. "It's just family, there's kinship ties," Martin said. MIDDLE EAST Martin said Ireland's peace-process experience also informs its approach to the Middle East, where Dublin has emerged as one of Israel's strongest European critics. He condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to security while arguing that the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza had been "absolutely disproportionate." "We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way." Martin said Ireland's strongly anti-Israel position was shaped partly by its own history and what he described as a "sense of right and justice and fairness." WATCH: Irish PM explains Ireland's position on Israel, rejects antisemitism concerns amid controversial soccer match TRUMP'S INVESTMENT PUSH HITS EUROPE AS IRISH PM EYES NEXT TARIFF BREAK EUROPE'S SECURITY Ireland currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, placing Martin at the center of negotiations as Europe confronts its biggest security challenges in decades. "There's a big realization in Europe that we have to do more to provide greater security to Europe, particularly because of the Russian-Ukrainian war," Martin said. He pointed particularly to Baltic and Nordic countries, where governments have increased defense spending amid fears about Russia. "Many have an existential fear of Russia," Martin said. Martin said Europe was also tightening its approach to immigration, echoing comments he made elsewhere in the interview that asylum applications had fallen across Ireland and that governments across the continent were responding to mounting political pressure. "The world needs to try and turn a page towards a more peaceful sort of coexistence," Martin said. WATCH: Irish PM explains how Ireland is responding to Trump's 'America First' agenda

articles.title: Mother, son among six identified after Boston-bound medevac jet vanishes off Nantucket
articles.summary: The six people aboard the Latitude Air Ambulance medevac jet that vanished over the Atlantic near Nantucket while en route to Boston have been identified.
articles.body: The six people aboard a Boston-bound medical jet that disappeared over the Atlantic have been identified as a Bermudian mother and son and a four-person Canadian flight and medical crew. Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, was being transported for treatment related to a stroke, with her son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, accompanying her aboard the medevac flight. The U.S. Coast Guard identified the four Canadians aboard as Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. 1 MISSING, 4 RUSHED TO HOSPITAL AFTER HELICOPTER CRASHES OFF SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ISLAND Childerhose was the captain and Farquhar was the first officer, while Paton served as the flight nurse and Weir as the respiratory therapist, according to Latitude Air Ambulance. The Gulfstream G100 disappeared early Saturday while traveling from Bermuda to Boston, triggering a major Coast Guard search off Nantucket. The Coast Guard suspended the search Sunday after debris associated with the aircraft was located. Lottimore was senior vice president and head of specialty reinsurance at Hamilton Re, according to the Bermuda-based company. "The entire Hamilton team is heartbroken by the loss of a respected leader, colleague and friend," Hamilton Re said in a statement. 4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS Lottimore was also a 2002 graduate of Warwick Academy, where he had served as a prefect. The school remembered him as an "outstanding person." Bermuda Police said a family liaison officer had been assigned to assist the family. The aircraft was operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, a Canadian medical transport company. Latitude previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that the Gulfstream was operating as a medevac flight and was expected to make the journey from Bermuda to Boston in approximately two hours. Latitude Air Ambulance President Peter Byl said the company was mourning an "unimaginable loss." "Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities," Byl said. "We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day." The flight departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport late Friday night and was bound for Boston Logan International Airport. COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said the crew reported electrical difficulties as the aircraft approached the Boston area before the jet descended rapidly and air traffic control lost contact south of Nantucket. FlightAware data previously reviewed by Fox News Digital showed the aircraft descending from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in roughly three minutes around 1 a.m. Saturday. The Federal Aviation Administration previously told Fox News Digital that it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at approximately 1:20 a.m. ET. Massport later confirmed the aircraft never arrived at Boston Logan. A civilian vessel located debris associated with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. "During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard Northeast District, said Monday. "We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation," Lake added. Canada is leading the investigation because the aircraft was registered there, in accordance with international agreements, according to the TSB. The National Transportation Safety Board is assisting as an accredited representative for the United States. The cause has not yet been determined. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The U.S. Coast Guard and Bermuda Police did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for additional comment Tuesday.Fox News Digital's James Cirrione contributed to this report.

articles.title: A storm cut off an Outer Banks couple from most of their wedding guests; they posted an open invitation online, and more than 400 strangers showed up with food, music and cameras to celebrate
articles.summary: After a storm stranded their guests, a couple posted an open invitation online, leading to hundreds of strangers celebrating their wedding on Hatteras Island with food, music, and love.
articles.body: Kimberly Laprad and Jayden Sink thought their wedding might end up as little more than a private photo session after a storm stranded most of their guests off North Carolina’s Outer Banks. Instead, hundreds of strangers turned up to celebrate with them.The couple had spent a year planning their Sept. 25 wedding on Hatteras Island, hoping to exchange vows on the beach. They had an indoor backup plan, but a nor’easter brought conditions far worse than expected. Road access to the island was cut off and officials declared a state of emergency, leaving most of their 45 invited guests unable to reach the wedding, according to The Washington Post.Laprad and Sink, both 24 and living in Roanoke, Virginia, had already made it to the island. Their vendors, including the musicians, cake provider, officiant and photographer, began cancelling as conditions worsened.“It wasn’t just disappointing,” Sink said. “It was defeating.”The couple invited the whole islandThe couple considered chartering a boat to bring their guests across, but abandoned the idea because conditions were too dangerous.With their plans collapsing, they considered putting on their wedding clothes and taking photographs themselves.“It would just have been a really expensive photo shoot,” Sink said.Then Laprad suggested something unexpected the night before the wedding.“Let’s just invite the whole island,” she told Sink.The idea started as a joke, but a friend who had reached the island before access was blocked began sharing an invitation in local Facebook groups.Within about 20 minutes, hundreds of people said they planned to attend. Dozens also offered food, cake, music and photography.“We thought maybe 20 or 30 people would show up,” Sink said. “We didn’t think it would go viral.”The couple had originally planned to hold their wedding at the beachfront property they had rented. With hundreds of strangers interested in attending, they needed a bigger venue.Local residents step inStacey Saunders, general manager of Frisco Woods Campground, saw the Facebook post and offered the couple the campground’s 38-acre property and pavilion for free.Saunders, who has managed the campground for five years, is also an ordained minister and offered to officiate.“I saw their Facebook post, and I was like, ‘I have the place, I have the means; if they can get to me, I can help them,’” she told the outlet..Restaurants and caterers donated food, people brought several wedding cakes, and three photographers, a DJ and a florist provided their services for free.Hatteras Island has about 4,000 year-round residents, but the wedding drew far more people than the couple had expected. Laprad and Sink estimated that between 500 and 800 people attended, while about 460 strangers signed their guest book.“Twenty four hours ago, we were all strangers,” Saunders said while officiating. “Now, we’re not.”A wedding they never expectedAmong the volunteers was Gwenyth Airhart, a professional wedding photographer from Luray, Virginia, who was vacationing on the island. After seeing a Facebook post about the couple, she decided to photograph the wedding.“I just felt really bad for their situation, knowing how special a wedding is, and then just these extreme circumstances,” Airhart told the newspaper.She called it the most memorable wedding of her five-year career.“I loved watching the outpouring of love that these random strangers had for this wonderful young couple,” she said.Laprad, who grew up visiting Hatteras with her family, said the community had changed how she viewed the unexpected turn of events.“The people on this island have definitely restored our faith in humanity,” she said.The couple still wished their family and original guests could have attended, but said the wedding ultimately became something they would not have experienced otherwise.“I think it happened the way it was supposed to,” Laprad said. “We all had a great time.”“We made a lot of friends,” Sink said.The couple plans to return to Hatteras Island every year for their anniversary. They have also started an online fundraiser for a sidewalk construction project on the island to give back to the community.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
